sections.text: No man can attain freedom from activity by refraining from action; nor can he reach perfection by merely refusing to act.
He cannot even for a moment remain really inactive, for the Qualities of Nature will compel him to act whether he will or no.
कर्मेन्द्रियाणि संयम्य य आस्ते मनसा स्मरन्।
He who remains motionless, refusing to act, but all the while brooding over sensuous objects, that deluded soul is simply a hypocrite.

We have completed chapter two, Sankhya Yoga, Yoga of Knowledge, in which we have seen that in the beginning Arjuna was confused about his duties. He wanted to act according to his Dharma, but he wasnt sure what is his Dharma. So he argued first that maybe I should not take part in this war because I dont want to be the cause for all the consequences of this bad war.
And then obviously he put for all his arguments, seeking endorsement from Krishna, that yeah, thats the right thing to do, lets stop this war. You run away and well be fine. Well, Krishna did not endorse his ideas and actually asked him to do his duties as the commander of the army, the Kshatriya.
To explain why Arjuna should fight, Krishna gave him a true thumbnail picture of who we are and how you should look at the world. So in the beginning he told him about what the self is, that this self is immutable, imperishable, only the body dies, and therefore you should not grieve about anybody dying. And then he continued telling him why he should continue his duty in this world.
But then Arjuna asked, is there any person who can be such established in this knowledge that he is equanimous? In the end we have seen that a man of a steady wisdom, how he lives his life in a very intelligent way, that he does not get affected by all the attractions of this objective world. So he always keeps his senses under control and remain equanimous mentally in all situations. And therefore Bhagavan said, you go ahead and act in this world, keeping your mind and intellect equanimous in all situations.
Now this seems very simple and clear to us, but Arjuna, who was truly in that dilemma of what is right, I want to do my Dharma, but I dont know which one is right. This whole discourse about what the self is all about obviously did not make it very clear to Arjuna. So the chapter three, titled Karma Yoga, Yoga of Action, now elaborates upon what is action and how you should work in this world.
You have to work in this world because we are all working. But if we find out how to act maybe we have a better results because we act in this world with mixed results. Sometimes we are successful, most of the time we are not.
Most of the time the results come completely contrary to what we think we should be getting out of our actions. So this chapter teaches us how to act in this world so our actions can be very effective. So the karma becomes Karma Yoga.
Therefore this chapter is very very popular. Some of the great commentators have said the Gita is all about Karma Yoga. It teaches you how to act in this life one way or other.
It is a very important chapter for all of us because all of us are trying to figure out how to work in this world because we will not be able to avoid working in this world. So the chapter opened with Arjunas question just as we all have. We all ask this question and say, yeah, this is great.
In the Gita class we talk about all this -- desirelessness and actionlessness -- and then go back to your workplace on Monday morning and try to tell that to your client. From our perspective it does not work. I actually just heard that Mina watches this course in the morning, so I get the benefit.
When Im passing around, I overhear stuff. Deepak bhai from Dada Bhagavan -- they have a question-answer format. So somebody asks, Deepak bhai, when I am trying to focus more on this Prateekraman and spirituality, I lose my motivation to make progress in my job.
Should I focus more on this or focus more on my job? Deepak bhai said, So whats your name, sir? My name is Janakbhai. Janakbhai, let Janakbhai make the progress in the job, and you establish yourself in spirituality. In other words, you need to separate yourself from whats happening in this world with you.
You become a sakshi-chaitanya. Basically, when you take the role of Janakbhai as an employee, you have to work as an employee very effectively. When Janakbhai is in spirituality, Janakbhai has to establish himself in spirituality.
So the answer is not very clear, and Janakbhai can say, Deepak bhai, tell me one thing -- you are not helping me here. Janakbhai is one, and you are telling me to be two different Janakbhais! So this is not Janakbhais newly minted question. This question Arjuna had 5,000 years ago. So he said, Jayasi Chit Karmanaste Mata Buddhi Janardina Tatkim Karmani Ghore Maam Niyo Jayasi Keshava.
You just discussed in detail what is right and what is wrong, what is better and what is not so good, what is higher and what is lower. In last chapter he says Durena hi Avaram Karmaha Buddhi Yoga Dhananjaya. Krishna in last verse clearly says that Karma is inferior to Buddhi Yoga.
In the beginning he propagated, you should go and fight for all these good reasons. Then he came back and said, you achieve the Buddhi Yoga. Buddhi yoga knowledge about what is your true self.
Arjuna said, thats what I was trying to do. I want to run away and meditate. If you consider that Buddhi is better than Karma, you say it very clearly.
In last chapter in verse 49, the Durenahiyavaram Karmaha Buddhi Yoga Dhananjaya. So therefore you said engage yourself in a Buddhi Yoga. You clearly told me that Tatkim Karmani Ghore mam.
Then why are you asking me to fight this war? This is like a person interested in physics who wants to find out what light is all about. If I ask a Mahatma like Sid Carey, who is a physicist, Tell me, sir, what is light? And he said, light can be a particle or a wave. I said, what do you mean? Is it a particle or a wave? Please dont confuse me.
He said, no, both are right. Except that you have to rise yourself to a level in your understanding to understand both viewpoints. He said it depends on the observer.
Observer can decide its a particle or its a wave. So Bhagavan said, karma is necessary, but Buddhi Yoga is also necessary. One is superior than other depending on where you are.
Vya Mishrena Vakhena Buddhim Moha Yasi Evame. This mixed Mishrena you are going the two mixed messages. You are speaking from both sides of your mouth.
One side saying go fight the war, thats okay, kill those people. Other side says, establish yourself in Buddha knowledge. This is confusing my intellect.
These statements have already confused my intellect. Tad Ekam Vadanishchtya. Therefore obviously I am your Srishya.
I already told you I am your Shishya. You tell me what is good for me. So dont go into this great arguments about which one is better.
Tell me one thing that will be the best for me which will be Shreyas which is good for me. As you are saying shres and prayers. Something which is pleasant but may not be good for me -- but something you tell me, it may not be pleasant, but tell me this is good for you.
And I already told you, I surrender to you. I will do whatever you tell me. And then comes the whole of Chapter 3, Karma Yoga.
Bhagavan said, Sri Bhagavanu Vacha. Now Bhagavan is elaborating on what Karma is all about. Loke Asmin Dvividha Nistha Pura Prukta Maya Anaga -- dont get confused.
There is not only one path in this world. Loki Asmin -- in this world. Dvivida Nishta -- I have established two paths.
Because you need to give people alternatives. You have to have choice. Pura Prokta Mayan -- right from the beginning, I established two paths.
This is the first time, as lots of commentators say, that Bhagavan comes out clearly and says, Im not Vasudeva Krishna. I am the Supreme Lord. That right from the beginning of this world, I established two paths. So you always had two options available from the day one.
The day I forgot myself as who I am. From the day I forgot that I am the Supreme Being and taken up this identity as me, this limited being, I had two paths available. Loki Asmin Dyudanista My loka started when the very first thought that I am who I am, this limited being.
And Bhagawan says there are always two paths available. It is like Im going to New York. My goal is to reach New York, and just around the Delaware, there are two paths.
One goes to the New Jersey Turnpike, another is 95 going through Philadelphia and all that. I get confused and say which way Im going. Well, I have two paths available.
I can go through the 95 and I still reach New York. And I can go through New Jersey Turnpike and Ill still reach New York. So Tupa is always available to me.
Gnana Yogina Sankhyana for those who are established in contemplation, those who are contemplative type. For them Gnana Yoga Yoga of Knowledge, Karma Yogi and a yoginand. Those who are action oriented.
For them Karma is established. Two paths are available to us. Either you have to work through your way to your goal or realize how to get there quickly.
If I realize the New Jersey Turnpike will be quicker and Ill take quicker path. If not, Ill work through my way through 95, going through the smaller town, all of that and traffic then reaching both will lead me. There is also something similar in our Indian system of marriage.
In the Indian system, I say, well, if you want to get married, you have two paths. Im not sure what is there now. Either you can have a love marriage.
You fall in love, find somebody and then get married. Or arranged marriage -- find somebody, get married, and then fall in love. Both ultimately culminating into what? One starts out by knowing first who I want to marry.
Knowledge occurs to me -- that one I like -- and then I get married. But then I work towards how to live together, what marriage is all about. All that takes place after Meena said, I never knew youre this swaroopa till I got married.
Even though we were dating for three years. On the other hand, you get married to somebody, you work through an arranged marriage. Then you have to fall in love with her.
The ultimate goal is to identify. Right now, my identification is with this limited self. My goal is to identify with the supreme self.
So identification has to change. When identification occurs, it becomes love. When I start identifying, then only I can love somebody.
I cannot love someone I never met. So I have to first know someone to fall in love with her. You fall in love, you rise in devotion.
So to love someone, you have to know the person. So to love the divine, you have to know the divine, that bhakti. Eventually youre trying to achieve the Bhakti Yoga.
Thats your goal, to have devotion for the Lord. But I cannot devote to somebody whom I do not know. I love God, but I dont know who.
That is not possible. So I have two paths to achieve that devotion. When I get the knowledge that who I am, that I am not this limited self, contemplating on who I am not, and I get the knowledge who I am, then Ill identify with that self.

These verses expose one of the most common spiritual traps: the pretense of renunciation. Krishna warns against the mithyachara - the hypocrite who outwardly restrains his senses while inwardly dwelling on sense objects. How often do we physically step away from temptation while our mind continues to feast on it? The person who refuses to eat cake but spends hours thinking about it has not truly renounced anything. The struggle has simply moved from the external to the internal realm.
The teaching here is liberating: you cannot achieve freedom from action (naishkarmya) by simply refusing to act. The qualities of nature - sattva, rajas, and tamas - will compel you to act whether you wish to or not. Even breathing, thinking, and sitting are actions. The path to liberation lies not in suppression but in transformation of how we act.
Today, honestly examine one area where you may be practicing this spiritual hypocrisy. Perhaps you have given up a habit outwardly, but your mind still gravitates toward it. Or maybe you have withdrawn from a responsibility while telling yourself it is detachment. True renunciation is internal - it means engaging fully with life while remaining mentally free. Ask yourself: Where am I restraining my body while my mind runs wild? What would it look like to act fully in that area while cultivating genuine inner detachment?
